Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Sunit is a 34-year-old South Asian male who works as a delivery driver. He is married and has been seeking psychological help after experiencing significant distress following a traumatic event that occurred six months ago. On his way to deliver packages in a busy urban area, Sunit accidentally caused a serious injury to another person when he lost control of the vehicle briefly due to a mechanical failure. The injured individual was taken away in an ambulance with critical injuries, and since then, Sunit has been grappling with overwhelming guilt and self-blame. The traumatic event itself was seared into his memory, replaying vividly whenever he closed his eyes or encountered any stimuli reminiscent of the accident. Every time he saw a delivery van on the road or heard the sound of screeching tires, Sunit would be transported back to that fateful day, reliving the moment when he felt utterly powerless to prevent the injury. He was certain that if he had been more vigilant or taken different precautions, such as performing regular maintenance checks, the accident could have been avoided. The guilt and self-blame were paralyzing for Sunit. He found himself constantly ruminating on what he should have done differently, replaying the scenario in his mind over and over again. "I should have protected others," he would tell himself, feeling like a failure because he had not prevented the injury. This belief was so entrenched that it affected almost every aspect of his life. Sunit began to avoid driving altogether, even for personal errands or short distances within his neighborhood. His job as a delivery driver became increasingly difficult and stressful. He started showing up late for deliveries or avoiding them entirely, leading to strained relationships with both his employer and colleagues. "I will never forgive myself for not doing more," he would think, each day feeling like an insurmountable burden. His marriage also suffered as Sunit withdrew emotionally from his wife. He found it hard to engage in normal conversations about work or daily life because they often triggered memories of the accident. What frightened him most was that he felt unworthy and unable to cope with everyday responsibilities, causing a rift between him and his spouse. His wife noticed a significant change in his demeanor—Sunit became distant, preoccupied, and often depressed. Over time, Sunit's occupational performance declined significantly. He had missed several deadlines and received warnings from his employer about his poor attendance. The guilt was so overwhelming that he began to consider quitting his job entirely, fearing that any mistake could lead to another accident. However, the thought of unemployment only deepened his sense of failure and self-doubt. Finally, after months of suffering in silence, Sunit's wife encouraged him to seek help from a therapist. She recognized how much pain he was in and urged him not to bear it alone any longer. Sunit’s most profound fear is that he will never be able to forgive himself or move past the guilt. At the same time, he hopes that therapy might provide some relief and allow him to reconnect with his family and regain a sense of purpose. In therapy, Sunit expresses his deep-seated belief that the event happened because of how he acted—this self-blame is not just an abstract feeling but a lived experience that shapes every decision he makes. He hopes that through understanding and processing this trauma, he can find some measure of peace and forgiveness, both for himself and from those around him who have been affected by his actions.
